clue.text: Threat to informer?

definitions.meaning: Said to a snitch rather than a customer, the advertising line stops being an invitation and turns into a warning about how long the grassing will go on.
The surface is selling you a day at the mall, but in British slang to grass somebody up is to 'shop' them, and that is the sense the first word carries.

explanation.walkthrough: Vlad turns a shop-window slogan into menace by changing what one verb means. There is no wordplay to unpick here — the whole clue is the joke, and spotting it is the solve.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase works as a threat because 'shop' means to grass someone up, so the shopping slogan reads as a promise of informing until you collapse.

clue.text: Youth is speaking about another: 'Dickhead!'

indicators.note: A story written about a subject goes all the way round it, and that is what the outer word does to the letters dropped between its ends.

parts.note: somebody who is speaking says
another of what the clue has just called a youth is a lad
the first letter of Dick — its head

explanation.walkthrough: The rudeness is a red herring: only the head of the name Dick is wanted. And 'another' leans on the definition, because another youth is simply a lad.
explanation.definitionFit: Salad days are the green, inexperienced years Cleopatra looks back on in Shakespeare, so the phrase is an idiom for being young rather than a plain synonym.

clue.text: B-list occasionally spoken about is going round

indicators.note: To be about a thing is to be all round it, so the longer piece closes over the shorter one.

parts.note: an oral exam is a spoken one

indicators.note: Something done occasionally happens every so often rather than every time, so only every other letter is picked up.

parts.note: every other letter of B-LIST: B, I and T

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is showbiz chatter and both instructions pass as ordinary description. Watch 'spoken': here it is a straight synonym, not an invitation to listen.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything orbital travels a circular path around something else — the motorway that rings London is called the orbital for exactly that reason.

clue.text: Singer Tom with suite trashed

indicators.note: To trash a hotel room is to leave nothing where it was, and letters treated that way come back in a different order.

parts.note: three of the eight letters, taken as they stand
the other five letters of the fodder

explanation.walkthrough: A rock star and a wrecked hotel suite make a perfectly good sentence, which is the point — neither word is doing the job it appears to be doing.
explanation.definitionFit: A titmouse is a small songbird, the tit of British gardens, so 'Singer' points at it by what the bird does rather than naming the family.

clue.text: I get emotional about returning to London's original theatre

indicators.note: original takes the first letter of London

parts.note: London's supplies its opening letter

indicators.note: returning, in a down clue, means the cry-around-I result reads upwards
about means the cry word goes around I

parts.note: to cry is to get emotional

explanation.surface: I get choked up going back to the first theatre in London.
explanation.walkthrough: CRY 'about' I gives CIRY, 'returning' gives YRIC, after L. The Lyric is a West End theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lyric is a well-known London theatre on Shaftesbury Avenue, a name used by many playhouses.

clue.text: Long for a drink?

parts.note: a yard is a long measure, three feet of it
the two prepositions swap freely when a vessel is named by what it holds
ale is the drink being measured out

explanation.walkthrough: Every word works twice: read straight it is a thirsty sigh, read as instructions it builds the thing itself. A clue that is all definition and all wordplay is called an &lit.
explanation.definitionFit: A yard of ale is the yard-long glass, and the beer in it, that pubs keep for challenges — so the clue describes it exactly: something long, for drinking.

clue.text: Turn left, perhaps, after park entrance — positive?

definitions.note: a noun: the positive aspect of something

indicators.note: the park letter is placed after the turn letter in the answer

parts.note: a U-turn, so Turn gives the letter U

indicators.note: the entrance to a word is its opening letter, so only the start of park is used

parts.note: first letter of park
left is one side, so this is SIDE by example

explanation.surface: Driving directions: turn left once you have gone past the park gates, with a hopeful query at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' gives U (as in U-turn), then P from 'park entrance', then SIDE, of which left is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The upside of a situation is its good or favourable aspect, a plus point; the question mark admits the loose fit.

clue.text: Complaining in bar

definitions.meaning: to rail at something is to complain loudly about it
a piece of ironmongery: the bar-work guarding a staircase or a balcony

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, no wordplay and two meanings of one word: a verb of protest and a piece of ironmongery. The little 'in' is all that joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: To rail at somebody is to complain bitterly, and a railing is the bar-work of a fence — one word, a verb sense and a noun sense.

clue.text: Forces serviceman, might you say?

definitions.meaning: Read straight this is any enlisted member of the armed services, which is the picture the surface wants: a soldier, a sailor, an airman.
The question mark admits the pun. The man meant is the one who takes the service — the chaplain attached to a regiment, and no fighting man at all.

explanation.walkthrough: Everything turns on the word 'service': the Forces have one meaning for it and the chapel quite another, and the answer is the man who belongs to both.
explanation.definitionFit: British soldiers borrowed the Spanish and Italian word for father to name their chaplain, so this is Forces slang for him rather than an official rank.

clue.text: Throw back nameless catch at sea

indicators.note: Something nameless has had its name taken off it, and the abbreviation for name is the single letter N.

parts.note: to lob a ball is to throw it
the stern is the back end of a boat

explanation.walkthrough: 'Throw back' reads as one action and is two separate jobs, which is the whole difficulty. N for name is worth learning: setters delete it constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: A lobster is literally a catch — what comes up in the pots — so the definition names the answer by the trade that lands it.

clue.text: Withdraw having committed a further offence as reported

indicators.note: Anything reported is passed on by mouth, so what matters is how the phrase sounds and not how it is written down.

parts.note: to sin again is to re-sin, so somebody who has offended a second time has RE-SINNED

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that a second offence and a cancellation sound identical. RE- for 'again' is worth filing away, since setters lean on it constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: To rescind a rule is to cancel it officially, which is what 'withdraw' means when a body takes back something it has already issued.

clue.text: Newton going, 'You shouldn't point!'

indicators.note: Something going is on its way out, so the letter named beside it leaves the word it was sitting in.

parts.note: don't is what you say for you shouldn't
N is the symbol for the newton, the unit of force

explanation.walkthrough: Vlad hides a physicist inside a telling-off, and the exclamation mark helps by making the last word look like rudeness rather than punctuation.
explanation.definitionFit: A dot is a point in the typographical sense — the full stop, the decimal marker — rather than the sharp end of anything.

clue.text: Previously keeping flashy eroticist very happy

indicators.note: To keep something is to hold on to it, and a word that keeps another closes right around it.

parts.note: once means previously, as in once upon a time
a loud tie is a flashy one
Anaïs Nin, the diarist who wrote erotica

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as gossip about somebody's taste in books, and nothing in it hints at delight. Anaïs Nin is standing crossword currency: file the three letters away.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on cloud nine is the idiom for elation, a whole phrase meaning delighted where none of its three words says anything of the kind alone.

clue.text: Mainly competent rating

parts.note: able means competent
the main is the open sea, so the man described as 'mainly' is a man of the sea

explanation.walkthrough: The main is an old word for the open sea, and 'mainly' is pointing at that rather than at 'for the most part'. The surface passes as faint praise.
explanation.definitionFit: In the navy a rating is any sailor below officer rank, and the answer is one of those ranks — so the definition names the class it sits in.

clue.text: Hit wicket — AUS 1 down (spinner finally bowled over)

indicators.note: something hit is knocked about, so the letters that follow are scrambled
one down means one fewer, so the numeral's letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, then losing its I
the Roman numeral for one is I
taken as written

indicators.note: only the closing letter of spinner is used

parts.note: last letter of spinner

explanation.surface: A cricket scorecard: an Australian batter out hit wicket, one down, with the spinner's final ball causing it.
explanation.walkthrough: '1 down' takes I out of WICKET to leave WCKET; add AUS and R (the final letter of 'spinner') and 'Hit' shuffles the lot. Hit wicket is a cricket dismissal where batters knock over their own stumps.
explanation.definitionFit: Being bowled over is an idiom for being overwhelmed with amazement, the same feeling as awe.

clue.text: Knocked back the drink (over a gallon) for some considerable time

definitions.note: The answer is plural in form but names one unbroken stretch, which is why a singular phrase defines it: nobody waits for one age.

indicators.note: Knocking a drink back is swallowing it, but knocking anything back sends it the other way, so the letters run in reverse.
What is over something lies across it and covers it, so the shorter piece ends up tucked inside.

parts.note: the drink is the sea, as in falling into it
G is the abbreviation for gallon

explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface belongs in a pub and not one of them stays there: the drink is salt water, and knocking it back is an instruction rather than a swallow.
explanation.definitionFit: Ages is the everyday exaggeration for a long stretch — 'I waited ages' — so it matches the loose, unmeasured quantity the definition describes.

clue.text: Synonyms to begin with: fly, go off, make a run for it

indicators.note: The phrase asks for the start of the word in front of it, so its opening letter is all that survives.

parts.note: the opening letter of Synonyms
a ked is the wingless fly that lives on sheep
eggs that go off addle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Synonyms' is lovely misdirection: it promises a list of words meaning the same thing, and only its first letter is wanted. The ked is worth meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: To skedaddle is to clear off in a hurry, which is just what making a run for it describes — the American slang verb for a hasty exit.

clue.text: Call service engineers initially for correction

parts.note: REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British army service; initially means it comes first
to dial is to call on the phone

explanation.surface: Phone the service engineers first to get a fault corrected.
explanation.walkthrough: REME is the British Army's Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers; 'initially' puts it ahead of DIAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Remedial work is intended to put right a fault, so it is done for correction.

clue.text: Coming back discontented, negotiates very low price, a bargain

indicators.note: coming back means the two outer letters are read in reverse
discontented strips out the contents, the middle of negotiates

parts.note: negotiates supplies its first and last letters
1P, one penny, is a very low price, written IP

explanation.surface: Coming back unhappy, someone haggles a rock-bottom price, a real deal.
explanation.walkthrough: NS (negotiates 'discontented') 'coming back' gives SN, then IP (1p, one penny).
explanation.definitionFit: A snip is British slang for a bargain, something cheap at the price.

clue.text: Less sensible son gets involved making little difference

indicators.note: Somebody who gets involved is drawn into the middle of the business, and the letter goes the same way.

parts.note: the more inane a thing is, the less difference it makes
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.walkthrough: Comparatives are what make this work: definition and wordplay are both '-er' forms, which is easy to miss while the surface is busy being about a family.
explanation.definitionFit: Insaner is the comparative of insane, so 'less sensible' matches it grade for grade — one step further from sound judgement rather than the full condition.

clue.text: US comedian put away for drugs in decline

indicators.note: one thing standing for another, so the drugs are replaced by what was put away

parts.note: Ellen DeGeneres, the American comedian and talk-show host
E is ecstasy, so ES is drugs in the plural
to put away food is to eat it, past tense ATE

explanation.surface: A US comedian jailed on drug charges, a career in decline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put away' looks like jailing but means eaten: ATE takes the place of ES (ecstasy tablets) at the end of DEGENERES.
explanation.definitionFit: To degenerate is to deteriorate or worsen, which is what something in decline does.

clue.text: Current Republican leading on the surface is a moron

indicators.note: Whatever lies on the surface covers what is underneath, so one word closes over the two letters and hides them.

parts.note: the runner who is leading is ahead
I is the physicist's symbol for electric current
R is the standard abbreviation for Republican

explanation.walkthrough: Politics is the misdirection: the opening two words are not a person at all but two single letters, one out of physics and one off a ballot paper.
explanation.definitionFit: An airhead is somebody with nothing much between the ears, so 'a moron' matches it insult for insult in ordinary speech.

clue.text: A green revolution of sorts

indicators.note: A revolution turns everything over, and letters caught up in one do not come back in the order they went in.

parts.note: the six letters of the fodder

explanation.walkthrough: 'A green revolution' is a real phrase about farming, which is exactly why it does not look like six letters waiting to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Genera are the groups biology sorts living things into, one rank above species, so 'sorts' is the plural noun in its classifying sense.

clue.text: Loudly complain after sailors originally aboard leave port?

indicators.note: the sound-alike word follows the other part
a letter taken aboard sits inside the word for leave

parts.note: to desert is to leave or abandon

indicators.note: only the opening letter of sailors is used

parts.note: first letter of sailors

indicators.note: said out loud, so the complaint word becomes a word sounding the same

parts.note: to whine is to complain

explanation.surface: Sailors grumbling about going ashore when they leave port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'port' looks like a harbour but is the fortified wine, hence the question mark: port is an example of a dessert wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Port is a sweet fortified wine traditionally served at the end of a meal, a classic example of the category.

clue.text: Make editor ultimately responsible for such columns

definitions.note: The answer is an adjective naming a style of column, so the plural noun phrase points at the order the style belongs to rather than substituting word for word.

parts.note: do and make share the sense of performing a task

indicators.note: What comes ultimately comes at the end, so the final letter of the word beside it is the one taken.

parts.note: the last letter of editoR
i/c is short for in charge, which is what being responsible for something is

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an office row about who carries the blame. Learn i/c for 'in charge': two letters that hide easily inside an innocent phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Doric names the oldest and plainest of the Greek architectural orders, so 'such columns' points at a style of building rather than at any one pillar.

clue.text: Vlad's past being ideal

parts.note: the setter of this puzzle is Vlad, so Vlad's is I'm
something past happened ago

explanation.walkthrough: Setters sign their own clues: whenever a Guardian puzzle names its setter, read it as 'I'. It is the same convention as 'the setter' meaning ME.
explanation.definitionFit: In psychoanalysis an imago is the idealised picture of a parent carried into adult life, so 'ideal' is that technical noun rather than the everyday adjective.

clue.text: Take main road around valley

parts.note: R is the prescription sign for take, from the Latin recipe

indicators.note: Turning a thing around leaves it facing the other way, so those two letters are read in the opposite order.

parts.note: the A1 is the main road north, and its 1 is written as the letter I

explanation.walkthrough: Numbers standing in for letters is a Vlad habit: the 1 of the A1 is an I, exactly as the 1 in 14 down is. R for 'take' comes off a doctor's pad.
explanation.definitionFit: A ria is a river valley drowned by the sea, so 'valley' names the landform the answer is a flooded example of.

clue.text: Neither partner recalled mentioning bread lines

indicators.note: recalled means the partner word is called back, read in reverse

parts.note: nor is the partner of neither in neither ... nor

indicators.note: mentioning signals that the money word is spoken, not written

parts.note: dough is slang for money, as is bread

explanation.surface: Neither partner remembered talking about the bread for the rhymes.
explanation.walkthrough: NOR 'recalled' gives RON; DEAU is said like DOUGH, slang for money, as is 'bread'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rondeau is a short poem of set form with a refrain, so a set of verse lines.

clue.text: Flavouring from America is in demand

parts.note: A is the standard abbreviation for America

indicators.note: The smallest word in the clue is the instruction: one piece goes inside another, exactly as being in demand puts you within it.

parts.note: a demand is a need
the word itself, taken as two letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'In demand' is a phrase the surface needs and the wordplay pulls apart. The most ordinary word in the clue is the one carrying the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Aniseed is the seed of the anise plant, used to flavour drinks and sweets, so 'Flavouring' names it by the job it does in a kitchen.

clue.text: What Telford had a lot of to attract Romeo — sex

indicators.note: To attract a thing is to draw it in towards you, which is where that single letter finishes up.

parts.words: What Telford had a lot of
parts.note: Thomas Telford built the canals, so canal knowledge is what he had in quantity
R is Romeo in the radio alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Telford was the great canal engineer, and the joke is that fourteen letters of specialist expertise need only one more to turn into something quite different.
explanation.definitionFit: Carnal knowledge is the legal and biblical idiom for sexual intercourse, so the whole phrase means 'sex' where neither of its words does alone.
